Title:           Pyrolysis-Dependent Uncollided Neutron Transmission in Date-Palm Biochar/Epoxy Composites: A GEANT4 Study with2 MeV and Cf-252 Neutrons 
Subject:         Pyrolysis changes both the composition and physical structure of biochar, making it necessary to separate chemistry-driven neutron-transport effects from density and geometry effects. This computational study examines date-palm biochars produced at 300, 500, and 800 $^{\circ }$C as fillers in an idealized epoxy matrix. The principal 2 MeV comparison used ten independent $10^6$-history GEANT4 runs per material at 20 wt% filler, 5 cm thickness, and equal bulk density (1.25 g cm$^{-3}$). From BC300 to BC800, total forward track-length fluence increased by only 0.30%, whereas the fluence-weighted $H^*(10)$ response increased by 2.86%. A separate ten-replicate component campaign confirmed that the 2 MeV BC800--BC300 $H^*(10)$ difference ($+0.07986$ pSv primary$^{-1}$) was driven by increased uncollided-primary transmission ($+0.08398$ pSv primary$^{-1}$), while the collided-primary contribution decreased slightly ($-0.00422$ pSv primary$^{-1}$). For a representative $^{252}$Cf Watt spectrum, $H^*(10)$ increased by 2.98%, with 91.1% of the net increase arising from uncollided primaries. A $30\times 30$ cm$^2$ full-face geometry increased scattered buildup, yet 84.0% of the BC800--BC300 $H^*(10)$ increase remained attributable to uncollided primaries. Additional density, thickness, and loading sensitivities gave positive BC800--BC300 $H^*(10)$ contrasts under all tested conditions (1.18--8.24%), although the integral-fluence contrast was not universally positive. The model therefore supports a robust chemistry-related increase in high-energy primary survival while showing that the scattered-field partition and engineering performance remain geometry- and processing-dependent.
